Workers' Compensation Billing

A System Where Being Late Electronically Means Not Getting Paid at All

Workers' compensation billing covers care for on-the-job injuries, paid by an employer's workers' comp insurance carrier rather than standard health insurance. It runs on its own fee schedules, its own utilization review process, and increasingly, its own mandatory electronic submission systems that vary meaningfully from state to state.

More than 30 states now use or require the IAIABC Claims Electronic Data Interchange standard for workers' comp claim submission, and a growing number have moved from voluntary to mandatory electronic billing. New York's Workers' Compensation Board made electronic billing mandatory for all providers as of August 2025, with no exceptions for smaller practices. Miss that requirement and the payer has no obligation to reimburse a paper bill at all.

PMEX bills workers' comp claims through the correct electronic system for each state a provider practices in, tracks utilization review and authorization requirements, and follows every claim through to payment.

New York's Electronic Billing Mandate

What Every NY Provider Treating Injured Workers Must Know

Since August 2025, every workers' comp bill in New York must be submitted electronically to the payer, with no exception for small practices or low claim volume, and bill data must also be submitted to the Workers' Compensation Board in the required XML format.

XML Submission Format

Bills submitted to the WCB through one of its approved XML Submission Partners.

7-Day Acknowledgment

Insurers must acknowledge receipt of an electronic bill within a set timeframe.

No Practice-Size Exception

The mandate applies to any provider treating even a single injured worker.

120-Day Resubmission Window

A bill sent non-electronically can be corrected and resubmitted within 120 days of service.

Electronic Billing Requirements by State

New York Isn't the Only State That Mandates It

Provider & Payer Both Required

Minnesota, North Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia require both payors and providers to submit and accept bills electronically.

Payer Required to Accept

California, Illinois, Louisiana and Oregon require payors to accept electronic bills, giving providers a strong incentive to file electronically.

Requirements change over time and vary by claim type and payer. PMEX monitors each state's current rules as part of ongoing billing management.

Yes. As of August 2025, all workers' comp bills in New York must be submitted electronically, with no exception for small practices or low claim volume. Bill data must also be submitted to the Workers' Compensation Board in the required XML format.

The payer is under no obligation to reimburse a non-electronic bill and can return it with a notice indicating it was submitted incorrectly. In New York, the provider then has 120 days from the date of service to resubmit electronically for payment.

The International Association of Industrial Accident Boards and Commissions Claims Electronic Data Interchange standard is the national format most states use for workers' comp claim data. More than 30 states currently use or plan to use it.

Yes. PMEX bills workers' comp claims across every state a practice operates in, applying that state's specific electronic submission rules, fee schedules and utilization review requirements.

Utilization review is the process workers' comp payers use to confirm treatment is medically necessary and appropriate for the injury before authorizing it. Treatment provided without proper authorization risks denial regardless of how the bill is submitted.
